chapter.name: Reproduction: How Life Continues
chapter.blurb: How life continues across organisms: asexual reproduction through vegetative propagation, budding and spores; sexual reproduction in flowering plants through pollination and fertilisation; the trade-off between egg numbers and survival across animal groups; and, in humans, the male and female reproductive systems, gametogenesis, the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, childbirth, and informed choices about contraception and sexually transmitted infections.

scope_in.item: Asexual reproduction: vegetative propagation methods - cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture
Budding in yeast and hydra as asexual reproduction
Spore formation in fungi (Rhizopus, Aspergillus) and Louis Pasteur's germ theory of disease showing new life comes from pre-existing life
Mitosis as the basis of asexual reproduction, producing genetically identical offspring (clones)
Practical applications of asexual reproduction: tissue culture in banana farming; fungi's role in antibiotics (penicillin, amoxicillin) and degrading waste
Sexual reproduction involving two parents, and meiosis halving the chromosome number to form haploid gametes
Human chromosome number (23 pairs = 46) and how meiosis creates variation through the random mixing of characteristics
Parts of a flower: sepal, petal, stamen (filament, anther), pistil (stigma, style, ovary)
Pollination: self-pollination and cross-pollination, and Activity 11.6's finding that pollen transfer is necessary for fruit formation
Pollination strategies: wind (wheat, maize, rice), water (Vallisneria, Hydrilla), insect (sunflower, hibiscus, marigold) and bird pollination, and their distinguishing features
Fertilisation in flowering plants: pollen tube growth, fusion of gametes to form a zygote, the ovary developing into a fruit and the ovule into a seed
Plant breeding methods: selective breeding, artificial hybridisation and genetic engineering for improved crop varieties
External and internal fertilisation in animals
Variation in reproductive strategies among animals: egg numbers versus survival of young, a larval feeding stage versus direct development (Table 11.4)

Human reproductive maturity; the male reproductive system (testes, scrotum, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, prostate) and the female reproductive system (ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina)
Gametogenesis by meiosis in the testes and ovaries, and the differences between sperm and egg (Table 11.5)
Ovulation, fertilisation, zygote formation and implantation marking the beginning of pregnancy; In-vitro Fertilisation (IVF) as combining an egg and sperm outside the body
Menstruation: shedding of the uterine lining when an egg is not fertilised, the menstrual cycle's typical timing (21-35 days) and its span from puberty (10-14 years) to menopause (about 50 years)
Biological sex determination: the mother always contributes an X chromosome, the father contributes an X or a Y
Menstrual hygiene practices and destigmatising menstruation
Pregnancy: three trimesters, the embryo-to-foetus transition around the ninth week, and childbirth
A mother's health during pregnancy (diet, check-ups, rest, avoiding harmful substances) and post-partum depression as a recognised, treatable condition
Sexual maturity versus emotional maturity during adolescence
Sexually Transmitted Infections (gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, HIV/AIDS) and how they spread
Contraceptive methods: barrier (condoms, vaginal covers), hormonal pills, Intra-Uterine Devices (Copper-T), and surgical methods
Abortion as a surgical method generally limited to the first trimester, and the legal prohibition on prenatal sex determination in India to protect the sex ratio

concepts.name: Asexual reproduction: vegetative propagation, budding and spores
concepts.description: One parent produces genetically identical offspring without gametes, through vegetative propagation in plants, budding in yeast and hydra, and spore formation in fungi.
concepts.idea: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and produces offspring (clones) genetically identical to it, through mitosis.
concepts.rule: Asexual reproduction is seen in unicellular organisms (bacteria, amoeba, yeast), simple multicellular organisms (hydra, sponge) and many plants. Plants with fleshy underground stems, such as potato and ginger, sprout new plants without seeds; money plant and sugarcane stem cuttings grow into new plants; Bryophyllum leaves sprout tiny plantlets. This is vegetative propagation: new plants arise from the vegetative (growing) parts of a plant, involving only one parent and producing genetically identical individuals. Scientists and horticulturists have adapted this into methods of cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture, widely used in agriculture and horticulture to grow desirable crops on a large scale, including tissue culture propagation of banana. In hydra, repeated cell division at a specific site on the parent produces a small outgrowth called a bud, which enlarges and separates to live independently; this is budding, also seen in yeast. Fungi such as Rhizopus and Aspergillus reproduce by forming spores in huge numbers in a sac-like structure or on hyphae; spores are lightweight, usually single-celled, and float through the air until they find moisture and nutrients to germinate. For long, people believed living things arose spontaneously from non-living matter; Louis Pasteur's experiments proved new life always comes from pre-existing life, founding the germ theory of disease and strengthening the cell theory. Fungi also benefit society: they degrade organic waste and pollutants, help remove heavy metals from industrial waste, and are the source of antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin. In every organism studied here, the process behind asexual reproduction is mitosis, a cell division producing two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent, so the offspring are genetically identical clones.
concepts.example: A Bryophyllum leaf sprouts tiny plantlets that grow into new plants, all genetically identical to the parent.

concepts.name: Sexual reproduction and meiosis
concepts.description: Sexual reproduction combines gametes from two parents; meiosis halves the chromosome number so it does not double every generation, and its random mixing creates variation.
concepts.idea: Meiosis is a special cell division that forms haploid gametes from a diploid parent cell, and the random way chromosome pairs separate during meiosis creates variation among offspring.
concepts.rule: Sexual reproduction involves two parents, both contributing genetic material to the offspring. If each generation received the full set of chromosomes from both parents, the chromosome number would double every generation; this problem is solved by meiosis, a special cell division that reduces the chromosome number of a parent cell (diploid) to half (haploid) in the daughter cells, called gametes. In animals, male gametes are sperm and female gametes are eggs; in plants, the pollen grain carries male gametes and the ovule carries the female gamete (egg). Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total) in body cells; during meiosis, chromosomes of each pair separate so each gamete gets only one chromosome from each pair, giving every human gamete 23 chromosomes. In the bead activity, three pairs of beads represent three contrasting characters on three different chromosomes; picking one bead at random from each pair gives 8 possible combinations. Imagining this with 23 pairs of chromosomes, each carrying information for many characters, shows how this random mixing gives children a unique combination of chromosomes, making them genetically different from their parents and siblings. This variation is important for the survival of a species: it helps some individuals adapt better to changing environments (e.g. tolerating low oxygen at high altitude, digesting milk in adulthood) and, over time, contributes to evolution.

concepts.name: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
concepts.description: Flowers are the reproductive organs of angiosperms; pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, and fertilisation forms a zygote that becomes a seed inside a fruit.
concepts.idea: Pollination (self or cross) transfers pollen to a stigma; fertilisation follows when the male gamete in the pollen tube fuses with the egg cell, and the ovule becomes a seed while the ovary becomes a fruit.
concepts.rule: A complete flower has four parts: the sepal (outer whorl, protects the bud), the petal (coloured, attracts pollinators), the stamen (the male part: filament plus anther, which produces pollen grains containing male gametes), and the pistil (the female part: stigma, style and ovary, the ovary containing ovules with an egg cell each). In Activity 11.6, fruit formed in every treatment except where stamens were removed from the flower bud, showing that transfer of pollen from anther to stigma is necessary for fruit formation; this transfer is called pollination. Pollen transfer to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant is self-pollination; transfer to the stigma of a flower of a different plant of the same type is cross-pollination. Pollination depends on external agents: wind (wheat, maize, rice - light, small, numerous pollen grains and a long feathery stigma), water (Vallisneria, Hydrilla), insects (sunflower, hibiscus, marigold - bright, fragrant flowers with nectar, and large, sticky or spiny pollen matched to a sticky stigma), and birds (coral tree, hibiscus - visited by birds like sunbirds). Once pollen reaches a compatible stigma, it grows a pollen tube down through the style into the ovary; the male gamete moves through this tube and fuses with the egg cell in the ovule - this fusion is fertilisation, and it forms a zygote, which develops into an embryo. The ovary enlarges into a fruit, while the ovules develop into seeds. Wind-pollinated grasses release far more pollen per flower than insect-pollinated plants but produce far fewer seeds on average (Table 11.3); producing huge numbers of pollen grains can still be effective because pollination by wind is far less targeted than by an insect visit.
concepts.example: In a hibiscus flower, insects carry sticky pollen from the anther to a sticky stigma, and the pollen tube then carries the male gamete down to the ovule to fertilise the egg cell.

concepts.name: Sexual reproduction in animals: fertilisation and strategies
concepts.description: Animals show external or internal fertilisation, and species trade off egg numbers against parental protection to give young ones a chance to survive.
concepts.idea: External fertilisation (outside the body, in water) generally produces many eggs with low survival, while internal fertilisation (inside the female's body) generally produces fewer eggs with better protection and higher survival.
concepts.rule: In many aquatic animals such as frogs and most fish, fertilisation occurs outside the body: the female releases eggs into the water and the male releases sperm over them - external fertilisation. Although many eggs are laid, many are destroyed by water currents or eaten. In reptiles, birds and mammals, fertilisation takes place inside the female's body - internal fertilisation - and the chances of survival of the young are generally higher because the fertilised egg or embryo is better protected. Table 11.4 shows fish (100s-1000s of eggs, low survival) and frog (5,000-50,000 eggs, low survival) with external fertilisation, against lizard (2-20 eggs, moderate survival) and bird (1-15 eggs, moderate-to-high survival) with internal fertilisation. Fish, amphibians and insects lay eggs with just enough yolk to produce a larva, which hatches and gets nutrition by feeding on organic matter; once it has accumulated enough nutrition, it transforms into the adult body, as in butterflies and frogs. In contrast, reptile and bird eggs each contain enough yolk to nourish the developing embryo fully until it hatches as a young one, with no separate larval stage. In mammals, the zygote grows and develops inside the female's body; mammals typically feed their young via breast milk after birth, and some species need an extended period of post-birth care depending on how developed the young are at birth.

concepts.name: Human reproductive system and gametogenesis
concepts.description: The male and female reproductive systems produce gametes by meiosis; ovulation, fertilisation and menstruation form the monthly cycle of egg release, possible pregnancy, or shedding of the uterine lining.
concepts.idea: Gametogenesis in the testes and ovaries uses meiosis to form sperm and eggs; ovulation releases one egg a month, and if it is not fertilised the thickened uterine lining sheds as menstruation.
concepts.rule: The male reproductive system has testes (which produce sperm and a hormone controlling sperm production and puberty changes) inside the scrotum, which keeps them cooler than body temperature, needed for sperm formation. Sperm travel through the vas deferens, which opens into the urethra, a shared passage for urine and sperm; the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids that nourish and help sperm move. Each sperm has a head with genetic material and a tail for swimming. The female reproductive system has a pair of ovaries (producing eggs and hormones), oviducts (fallopian tubes) connecting each ovary to the uterus (where a foetus develops), and the uterus opens into the vagina through the cervix. Gametogenesis, the formation of gametes, happens in the testes and ovaries by meiosis; human body cells have 46 chromosomes, but sperm and eggs have only 23, so their fusion restores 46 in the zygote. Gametogenesis in males produces numerous tiny motile sperm; in females it produces a single large, non-motile egg with stored nutrients (Table 11.5). From puberty, usually one mature egg is released from an ovary every month - ovulation - while the uterus lining thickens to prepare to receive a zygote. During intercourse, millions of sperm may reach the egg in the oviduct; if one fuses with it, a zygote forms, undergoes mitotic divisions while travelling to the uterus, and implants into the thickened lining - marking the start of pregnancy. In-vitro Fertilisation (IVF) combines an egg and sperm outside the body, usually in a lab dish, before implanting the result in the uterus. If the egg is not fertilised, it degenerates within about a day; the thickened, no-longer-needed uterine lining sheds along with some blood through the vagina - menstruation, usually lasting 3-7 days. This ovulation-preparation-menstruation cycle typically repeats every 21-35 days (often about 28 days), from puberty (10-14 years in girls) until menopause (about age 50). The mother always contributes an X chromosome to a baby; the father contributes either an X (giving a girl, XX) or a Y (giving a boy, XY).
concepts.example: About once a month from puberty onwards, one mature egg is released from an ovary; if it is not fertilised, the thickened uterine lining sheds as menstruation.

concepts.name: Pregnancy, childbirth and reproductive health
concepts.description: Human pregnancy lasts about nine months across three trimesters; a mother's health, sexual and emotional maturity, and informed choices about contraception and STI prevention are all part of reproductive health.
concepts.idea: Pregnancy progresses through three trimesters to childbirth, and reproductive health includes a mother's care during pregnancy, understanding sexual versus emotional maturity, and using contraception to prevent unwanted pregnancy and infections.
concepts.rule: Human pregnancy lasts about nine months, divided into three trimesters. In the first trimester, the fertilised egg develops into an embryo over the first two months, with major organs starting to form; from about the ninth week it is called a foetus. In the second trimester, the foetus grows bigger and stronger, and movements can usually be felt. In the third trimester, the baby grows rapidly and prepares for birth. During childbirth, uterine muscle contractions push the foetus out through the birth canal; sometimes medical or surgical delivery is needed. After birth, breastfeeding is essential for complete nutrition and disease protection; newborns need warmth, timely vaccination and gentle handling. The mother needs a balanced diet, regular check-ups, rest, and to avoid smoking, alcohol or unprescribed medicines; post-partum depression is a recognised, treatable condition, and mothers should be encouraged to talk to a healthcare worker if they feel low or overwhelmed. Sexual maturation (like sperm production in boys and menstrual cycles in girls) develops gradually during adolescence, but this does not mean full readiness for adult responsibilities; emotional maturity - handling feelings, communicating clearly, making thoughtful decisions - takes longer to develop. Since sexual activity involves close physical contact, Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) - such as gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts and HIV (which can lead to AIDS) - can be transmitted, and some are not yet curable; condoms can prevent transmission and also help prevent pregnancy. Contraceptive methods include barrier methods (condoms, vaginal covers), oral pills (hormonal, may have side effects), Intra-Uterine Devices such as Copper-T (may sometimes irritate the uterus), and surgical methods (blocking the vas deferens or fallopian tubes). Unwanted pregnancy can also be ended by abortion, generally only within the first trimester, when the embryo is very small; self-selective (sex-based) abortion is a serious concern that can imbalance the societal sex ratio, so prenatal sex determination is strictly prohibited by law in India.
concepts.example: In the first trimester, the fertilised egg develops into an embryo and, from about the ninth week, is called a foetus, as major organs begin forming.
